deep_dive.title: Enabling Extended SGX Enclaves inside Confidential Virtual Machines
deep_dive.abstract: Confidential Virtual Machines (CVMs), such as AMD SEV-SNP, and process enclaves, such as Intel SGX, provide workload protection against cloud threats. However, they strongly differ in TCB, deployment cost and speed, peer workload protection, resource sharing, fine-grained isolation and attestation, and programming capabilities. Nesting process enclaves within CVMs offers an optimal solution and an opportunity to address long-standing SGX limitations: lack of intra-enclave protection, expensive transitions and exception paths, slow enclave cloning, and a restricted programming model that limits Library Operating Systems (LibOS).   This paper introduces TEEVisor, a CVM-resident architecture consisting of a security monitor and a kernel driver that leverages AMD SEV-SNP Virtual Machine Privilege Levels (VMPLs) to build hardware-protected, process-level enclaves inside a guest CVM with two modes: (1) an SGX binary compatibility mode to run unmodified SGX applications; and (2) a novel extended SGX~(eSGX) mode optimizing slow execution paths and offering richer enclave programming capabilities. On commercial AMD EPYC hardware, against native CVM execution, TEEVisor incurs under 5% overhead on compute- and memory-bound workloads, around 12% on I/O-heavy applications, and accelerates enclave cloning to a rate of 93~$μ$s/MB of enclave size, demonstrating that eSGX semantics inside a CVM are practical for production use.

quick_skim.title: ContractLens: Latent Security Knowledge for Malicious Smart Contract Detection
quick_skim.abstract: Detecting malicious smart contracts is essential to safeguarding the Web3.0 ecosystem. However, existing auditing methods based on large language models (LLMs) largely rely on prompt engineering or attack-specific fine-tuning, while the internal representations that support malicious logic detection remain poorly characterized. To address this gap, we propose ContractLens, a framework that localizes and uses latent security knowledge in pretrained LLMs for interpretable malicious smart contract detection. Specifically, we first use layerwise linear probes to identify candidate layers that distinguish malicious from benign contracts, then select critical layers based on their sensitivity to malicious logic removal and stability under behaviour-preserving surface modifications. Next, within these critical layers, we combine activation contrast, malicious-logic specificity, and probe weights into a tri-factor importance score and adaptively select malicious contract-discriminative units (MCDUs) using the knee point of the ranked score curve. Finally, we concatenate the selected units' activations into a compact representation and train a lightweight classifier for detection, keeping the pretrained model frozen throughout. Neuron masking experiments show that masking MCDUs causes larger drops in detection performance than masking randomly selected neurons or neurons matched in activation magnitude. ContractLens achieves higher average detection accuracy than the evaluated methods on all three pretrained models. Further evaluations demonstrate generalization to unseen malicious intents and show that, with the identified MCDUs fixed, a classifier trained on few labelled samples can still achieve strong detection performance.

quick_skim.title: Security Is More Than a Library Call: How Security Features Live in Code
quick_skim.abstract: Implementing security features---functionalities that protect sensitive data or prevent malicious actions by attackers---is important for ensuring the security and integrity of software systems. Correctly implementing access control, cryptography, or other security features is challenging as they require substantial domain expertise, careful design, and custom implementation to integrate them within the software system.   Previous work has thoroughly studied security awareness, perception, practices, and expertise via surveys, interviews, and experiments. While they have shown that the implementation of security features are often supported by security libraries and frameworks, they have also shown that developers rarely are security experts, and make mistakes that introduce vulnerabilities into software when using them. Despite this extensive knowledge of security practices and developer behavior, we still lack a comprehensive understanding of how security features actually manifest at the code level across full software systems.   We close this gap by conducting a mining study of security features in 9 popular and large open-source Java systems. We manually inspected 2,127,761 lines of code across 19,121 files, identifying and annotating 183,395 lines implementing 561 security features corresponding to 54 security features in our taxonomy. We analyzed the characteristics of the identified security features, such as their size, scattering, tangling, common implementation patterns, and the use of internal and external functionalities. Our findings show that security features are far more than mere calls to external libraries. Security features, such as access control, can grow large in size, scatter across the whole codebase, and frequently tangle with each other. External security libraries are commonly used, but they require substantial amounts of code for integration.
quick_skim.llm_evidence_en: how security features such as access control and cryptography are implemented in code
quick_skim.llm_evidence_cn: 访问控制与密码学等安全特性在代码中的实现

quick_skim.canonical_evidence: 访问控制与密码学等安全特性在代码中的实现
quick_skim.llm_tldr_en: Implementing security features such as access control and cryptography is hard and goes beyond calling libraries. This study examines how security features actually live in code, revealing the custom integration work and patterns behind correct implementation.
quick_skim.llm_tldr_cn: 实现访问控制、密码学等安全功能对软件系统安全至关重要，但其正确实现需要深厚领域知识、精心设计与定制集成，而开发者往往并非安全专家。本文研究安全功能如何在代码中实际存在与实现，分析其与安全库和框架的关系及常见实现模式。结果揭示了安全实现远不止一次库调用，往往需要大量定制代码。该工作为理解与改进软件安全特性的工程实践提供了实证依据。

quick_skim.title: Learning from Failures: A Failure-Driven Prompt Refinement for LLM-Based Vulnerability Analysis
quick_skim.abstract: Large Language Models have emerged as promising tools for software vulnerability analysis, but their effectiveness depends heavily on prompt design. Existing research primarily compares prompting strategies using aggregate performance metrics, providing limited insight into why models fail or how prompts can be improved systematically. We propose Failure-Driven Prompt Refinement (FDPR), a methodology that analyzes recurring model failures to guide evidence-based prompt refinement. Using the Damn Vulnerable Java Application (DVJA), we identify recurring failure modes, including false positives, false negatives, unsupported reasoning, and CWE misclassification, and translate them into targeted prompt refinements. We then evaluate the resulting prompt on the Juliet Test Suite and perform cross-model validation to assess generalizability. The results show that failure-driven refinement improves the reliability of LLM-based vulnerability analysis while yielding reusable prompt design principles. More broadly, this work demonstrates that recurring model failures provide a principled foundation for prompt engineering, enabling the systematic development of more reliable LLM-based vulnerability analysis systems.
quick_skim.llm_evidence_en: failure-driven prompt refinement for LLM-based vulnerability analysis

quick_skim.llm_tldr_en: FDPR analyzes recurring LLM failure modes in vulnerability analysis and converts them into targeted prompt refinements, improving detection reliability.

quick_skim.title: A Systematic Study of Security Enforcement at Android Inter-Component Boundaries
quick_skim.abstract: Android's inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms (Activities, Services, BroadcastReceivers, ContentProviders, and URI scheme handlers) form the primary interface between applications and between applications and the system. We present a systematic study of security enforcement comprising 120 evaluations (99 inter-component interface evaluations across five interface categories, 10 platform security-control evaluations, and 11 dedicated positive controls) in over 30 Google and AOSP packages on Android 17 (API 37). Using an expected-versus-observed framework under a zero-permission attacker model, we evaluate whether each boundary's enforcement mechanism functions as designed. We find 97 enforcement gaps (80.8%) and 23 enforcement holds (19.2%). From these observations, we derive a 14-category enforcement gap taxonomy organized across manifest, code, platform, and architectural layers. Within our purposively selected corpus, observed enforcement outcomes differ substantially across interface categories: evaluated Activities and BroadcastReceivers exhibit a 100% gap rate, while ContentProviders, which benefit from framework-provided defenses such as setStrict(), achieve a 27.6% holds rate. We find that all seven evaluated platform compatibility changes with security intent are either disabled or gated at a targetSdkVersion that none of the applications in our evaluated corpus targets. We document 18 custom URI scheme registrations handling sensitive data (authentication tokens, payment credentials, medical information) despite the known unverifiability of custom schemes (RFC 8252 Section 8.1). Our study includes 23 positive controls, calibration cases demonstrating that the evaluation procedure distinguishes functioning enforcement from observed enforcement failures.

quick_skim.title: ToFu: Exploiting and Fuzzing the LLM-Orchestrator-Tool Trust Boundary
quick_skim.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that interact with external software through tools, with an orchestration layer translating model outputs into structured tool invocations. This architecture creates an LLM-orchestrator-tool trust boundary where tool semantics may go unenforced and LLM-generated arguments may be incorrectly treated as trusted. We present ToFu, a tool-aware framework that automatically derives semantic security checks for LLM tools from their existing metadata and a CWE-guided sanitizer corpus. ToFu specializes these checks to individual tools and automatically generates fuzzing harnesses and semantic oracles using runtime introspection and outcome sanitization. We evaluated ToFu across 273 MCP servers containing 3405 tools and identified verified bugs corresponding to CWE weakness classes in 343 tools across 118 of the servers. Our findings show that real-world tools frequently fail to enforce their documented input semantics, making it unsafe to treat LLM-generated arguments as trusted.
quick_skim.llm_evidence_en: fuzzing and semantic security checks at the LLM-tool trust boundary
quick_skim.llm_evidence_cn: 在LLM-工具信任边界进行模糊测试与语义安全检查

quick_skim.llm_tldr_en: LLM agents invoke external tools through an orchestration layer that may not enforce tool semantics, treating model arguments as trusted. ToFu derives semantic security checks from tool metadata and a CWE-guided sanitizer corpus, then auto-generates fuzzing harnesses and oracles, evaluated across 273 MCP servers to expose trust-boundary flaws.
